In the long run it is a trade-off.
I joined the club team because I wanted to hear English all day.
Since nobody on the team spoke Portuguese, I had no easy way out.
Training took four evenings a week, so I studied after ten at night.
The whole season ran in English, which is why five months beat five years.
So you played a full season here and studied at the same time. Everyone says that is impossible. What is your point of view?
It is not impossible, it is a trade-off. I gave up my evenings, and I got a level of English I could not have got in a classroom.
I am not sure I buy that. Plenty of people take a language course and never touch a ball. Can you back that up?
Sure. In a course you speak for maybe twenty minutes a week. At training nobody waits for you, so you talk for two hours, four times a week. That is the evidence.
Fair. But my grades went down in my first season, and I know I am not the only one. Is that not a serious drawback?
It is, and I am not going to pretend it is not. Mine dropped too. But in the long run I got the grades back, and the English stayed.
That is the honest answer, and honestly it is the one nobody gives me. Most people just tell me sport builds character.
Because that is easy to say and impossible to prove. A number is harder to argue with. And you — how many hours a week does hockey take from you?
My point of view is that a season abroad teaches you more than a year of classes.
I say that because nobody on the team ever waited for me to translate.
Let me back that up: two hours of English, four times a week, for five months.
There is a real drawback, and it is a trade-off I would make again.
The strongest counter-argument is my grades, so let me answer that directly.

Every September a family sits in my office and asks me the same question, and I always answer it with a number before anything else. About twenty hours a week, once you count the travel. Eight hours of training, three on match day, four on the bus every second week, and five in study hall. I say it first because families find out anyway, usually in October, and it is better that they hear it from me in a quiet room. Then I tell them the second thing, which is harder to say out loud. Most first-year grades go down. Not all of them, but most. They come back up in the second year, and the students who leave the program almost always leave during that first bad term, before anything has had time to recover. What I refuse to do is argue that sport builds character, because I cannot measure character and neither can you. What I can measure is who finishes. Our athletes complete their degrees at a higher rate than the campus average, and they have done that for eleven years running. That is the argument I make, and it is the only one I need.

People always assume I left the team because I was not good enough, and I understand why, because that is the usual story. It is not what happened. I left because I wanted the engineering degree more than I wanted another season, and by the end of the second year those two things did not fit in the same week any more. Something had to go, and I chose. What surprises people is the next part. I do not regret the first year at all. My English came out of that year, and so did my confidence, because you cannot spend nine months on a bus with fourteen people and stay quiet. If somebody asked me today whether they should do one season, I would say yes without thinking about it. So the argument everybody has, about whether sport is good for students or bad for them, is the wrong argument. The real question is how long you keep doing it. One season is an investment. Four seasons is a career decision, and almost nobody talks about it that way.
